questions.q: In map reading, what does the term 'scale of a map' mean?
o: The size of the map compared to the size of the paper it is printed on
The distance on the map and the corresponding distance on the ground
The number of towns shown on the map compared to their real population
The height of contour lines compared to the actual height of hills
questions.e: Scale is the ratio that links a distance measured on the map to the actual distance it represents on the ground. It does not depend on paper size, population or heights.
questions.p: Scale na di relationship between distance wey dem draw for map and di real distance for ground. E no concern paper size, population or hill height.

questions.q: A map has a scale of 1:100000. If the distance between Oke-Ado market and Bodija market on the map is 3.5 cm, what is the actual distance between the two places on the ground?
questions.e: At 1:100000, 1 cm on the map equals 100000 cm (1 km) on the ground. So 3.5 cm on the map represents 3.5 cm x 1 km = 3.5 km on the ground.
questions.p: For scale 1:100000, 1 cm for map na 100000 cm (1 km) for ground. So 3.5 cm go be 3.5 km for ground.

questions.q: A topographical sheet has a representative fraction (RF) of 1:250000. Express this as a statement scale in the form '1 cm represents ___ km'.
questions.e: Divide 250000 cm by 100000 (the number of centimetres in a kilometre) to get 2.5. So 1 cm on the map represents 2.5 km on the ground.
questions.p: You go divide 250000 cm by 100000 (wey be how many cm dey for 1 km) to get 2.5. So 1 cm for map na 2.5 km for ground.

questions.q: A map is drawn to a linear scale of 1:20000. A cocoa farm is shown on the map as a shape covering 5 square centimetres. What is the actual area of the farm on the ground, in square kilometres?
questions.e: First change the linear scale to km: 1 cm represents 20000 cm = 0.2 km. The area scale is (0.2 km)^2 = 0.04 km^2 per cm^2. Multiply by 5 cm^2 to get 0.2 km^2.
questions.p: First convert di linear scale to km: 1 cm na 20000 cm = 0.2 km. Area scale na (0.2)^2 = 0.04 km^2 for every cm^2. Multiply by 5 cm^2, e go give 0.2 km^2.

questions.q: On the ground, two villages, Egbeda and Isale-Oyo, are 45 km apart. On a map, the distance between them is measured as 9 cm. What is the representative fraction (RF) of the map?
questions.e: Convert 45 km to centimetres: 45 x 100000 = 4500000 cm. Divide this by the map distance, 9 cm, to get 500000. So the RF is 1:500000.
questions.p: Change 45 km go cm: 45 x 100000 = 4500000 cm. Divide am by 9 cm (map distance), e go give 500000. So RF na 1:500000.

questions.q: A linear (graphical) scale on a map shows a straight line marked from 0 km to 60 km, and the total length of this line on the map measures 6 cm. What is the representative fraction (RF) of this map?
questions.e: Change 60 km to centimetres: 60 x 100000 = 6000000 cm. Divide this by the map length, 6 cm, to get 1000000. So the RF is 1:1000000.
questions.p: Change 60 km go cm: 60 x 100000 = 6000000 cm. Divide am by 6 cm (map length), e go give 1000000. So RF na 1:1000000.

questions.q: A map is drawn to a scale of 1:50000. On the map, a rectangular farmland owned by Alhaji Musa measures 4 cm by 3 cm. What is the actual area of the farmland on the ground, in square kilometres?
questions.e: At 1:50000, 1 cm represents 50000 cm = 0.5 km. So the sides become 4 x 0.5 = 2 km and 3 x 0.5 = 1.5 km. Multiply the two actual sides: 2 km x 1.5 km = 3 km^2.
questions.p: For 1:50000, 1 cm na 0.5 km. So di sides become 4 x 0.5 = 2 km and 3 x 0.5 = 1.5 km. Multiply di two sides: 2 km x 1.5 km = 3 km^2.

questions.q: A cartographer redraws an old map originally at a scale of 1:50000 by enlarging every linear measurement on it twice (so that a line that was 1 cm now becomes 2 cm), while the actual ground distances represented stay the same. What is the new scale of the enlarged map?
questions.e: Since the same ground distance is now shown by twice the map length, the map distance per unit ground distance has doubled, so the denominator of the scale is halved: 50000 / 2 = 25000. The new scale is 1:25000, which is a larger (more detailed) scale than the original.
questions.p: Since dem don enlarge di map but di real ground distance remain di same, di number wey dey behind di scale go reduce by half: 50000 / 2 = 25000. New scale na 1:25000, wey be bigger (more detailed) scale pass di first one.

questions.q: On a topographical map, a contour line is best described as a line that joins places of equal...
questions.e: A contour line links points on the map that have the same elevation above sea level. It is the standard way maps show relief without using pictures or shading.
questions.p: Contour line na line wey join places wey get the same height from sea level. Na so maps dey show relief without picture or shading.

questions.q: On a topographical map, contour lines that are drawn very close together (tightly packed) within a small area indicate that the land in that area has a...
questions.e: When contour lines are packed close together, it means height changes quickly over a short horizontal distance, which is the definition of a steep slope. Widely spaced contours would instead show a gentle slope.
questions.p: When contour lines close well-well for short distance, e mean say height dey change fast-fast, na so steep slope be. If contour lines dey far apart, na gentle slope.

questions.q: On a map drawn to a scale of 1:50,000, two points A and B are 6 cm apart. Point A is 150 m above sea level and point B is 450 m above sea level. What is the gradient between A and B, expressed as 1 in n?
questions.e: Ground distance = 6 cm x 50,000 = 300,000 cm = 3000 m. Vertical interval = 450 - 150 = 300 m. Gradient = ground distance / vertical rise = 3000/300 = 10, so the gradient is 1 in 10.
questions.p: Ground distance = 6 x 50,000 = 300,000 cm = 3000 m. Height wey dem climb = 450 - 150 = 300 m. Gradient = 3000/300 = 10, so na 1 in 10.

questions.q: A map shows a series of contour lines with the following successive values written on them: 100 m, 150 m, 200 m, 250 m. What is the contour interval used on this map?
questions.e: The contour interval is the constant difference in height between one contour line and the next. Here, 150 - 100 = 50 m, and this same gap (200-150, 250-200) is maintained throughout, so the interval is 50 m.
questions.p: Contour interval na the constant height gap between one contour line and the next one. 150 - 100 = 50 m, and the gap stay the same throughout, so the interval na 50 m.

questions.q: On a map, a group of contour lines form several concentric (nested) circles, one inside the other. The outermost circle is labelled 200 m and the value increases steadily to 400 m on the innermost circle. This pattern most likely represents...
questions.e: When contour values increase from the outside towards the centre of concentric circles, it shows the land is rising towards a high point in the middle, which is typical of a hill. A depression would show the opposite pattern, with values decreasing inward.
questions.p: When the contour numbers dey increase from outside go inside for nested circles, e mean say the land dey rise go up for the middle, na so hill be. If na depression, the numbers for inside go dey smaller.

questions.q: On a topographical map, contour lines are seen bending sharply to form a V-shape. The pointed tip of each V points towards the higher contour values (uphill), and a blue stream line runs through the point of the V. This feature most likely represents...
questions.e: When contours bend into a V that points towards higher ground and a stream flows through the bend, the land is cut by water flowing downhill, which is the classic sign of a river valley. A spur or ridge would instead show the V pointing towards lower ground (downhill).
questions.p: When contour dey bend like V wey dey point go higher ground, and river dey pass through the bend, na river valley be that, because water dey cut through as e dey flow down. Spur or ridge go show V wey dey point go lower ground instead.

questions.q: A map has a scale of 1:20,000. Two points, P and Q, are 5 cm apart on the map. P is 550 m above sea level while Q is 350 m above sea level. Calculate the gradient between P and Q, expressed as 1 in n.
questions.e: Ground distance = 5 cm x 20,000 = 100,000 cm = 1000 m. Vertical interval = 550 - 350 = 200 m. Gradient = 1000/200 = 5, so the gradient is 1 in 5, which is a fairly steep slope.
questions.p: Ground distance = 5 x 20,000 = 100,000 cm = 1000 m. Height difference = 550 - 350 = 200 m. Gradient = 1000/200 = 5, so na 1 in 5, e be steep slope small.

questions.q: If a point is situated exactly to the East of an observer, what is its bearing from the observer, measured clockwise from North?
questions.e: Bearings are measured clockwise from North (000°). East is a quarter turn (90°) clockwise from North, so the bearing is 090°.
questions.p: Dem dey measure bearing from North, go clockwise. East na quarter turn from North wey be 90°, so bearing na 090°.

questions.q: Town K is situated due South of town L. What is the bearing of K from L?
questions.e: South is a half turn (180°) clockwise from North. Since K is directly south of L, the bearing of K from L is 180°.
questions.p: South na half turn (180°) clockwise from North. Since K dey south of L, bearing of K from L na 180°.

questions.q: On a standard compass rose, which direction lies exactly halfway between North and East?
questions.e: The direction exactly between North (000°) and East (090°) is North-East, which corresponds to a bearing of 045°.
questions.p: The direction wey dey exactly between North and East na North-East, wey be bearing 045°.

questions.q: The bearing of a market square from Mrs Adeyemi's house is 065°. What is the bearing of the house from the market square?
questions.e: To find a back bearing when the given bearing is less than 180°, add 180°. So 065° + 180° = 245°, which is the bearing of the house from the market square.
questions.p: To find back bearing when the bearing dey less pass 180°, add 180°. So 065° + 180° = 245°, na so e be the bearing of house from market.

questions.q: A surveyor stationed at point P sights a flagpole at point Q on a bearing of 300°. What is the bearing of P as seen from Q?
questions.e: When the given bearing is greater than 180°, subtract 180° to get the back bearing. So 300° - 180° = 120°, which is the bearing of P from Q.
questions.p: When bearing pass 180°, you go minus 180° to get back bearing. So 300° - 180° = 120°, na im be bearing of P from Q.

questions.q: On a topographical map, eastings (vertical grid lines) are numbered 10, 11, 12, 13... from west to east, and northings (horizontal grid lines) are numbered 20, 21, 22, 23... from south to north. A health centre lies 4 tenths of a grid square east of easting line 14 and 6 tenths of a grid square north of northing line 23. What is the six-figure grid reference of the health centre?
questions.e: A six-figure grid reference states the easting first, then the northing, each refined to tenths. Easting 14 plus 4 tenths gives 144; northing 23 plus 6 tenths gives 236. Combined, the grid reference is 144236.
questions.p: Six-figure grid reference na easting first before northing, each one get tenths. Easting 14 plus 4 tenths na 144; northing 23 plus 6 tenths na 236. If you join am, e go be 144236.

questions.q: A topographical map has a scale of 1:25,000. If the actual distance between two adjacent grid lines on the ground is 1 km, what is the distance between the same two grid lines on the map, in centimetres?
questions.e: 1 km on the ground equals 100,000 cm. Since the scale is 1:25,000, the map distance is 100,000 / 25,000 = 4 cm.
questions.p: 1 km for ground na 100,000 cm. Since scale na 1:25,000, map distance na 100,000 divide by 25,000 wey be 4 cm.

questions.q: A ship sails from port A on a bearing of 040° for 60 km to reach port B. At B, it changes course and sails on a bearing of 130° for 80 km to reach port C. Calculate, to the nearest whole degree, the bearing of port C from port A.
questions.e: Since the course changes from 040° to 130°, the turn at B is a right angle (90°), making triangle ABC right-angled at B with legs 60 km and 80 km. The angle at A between AB and AC is arctan(80/60) = 53.13°. Adding this to the bearing of B from A (040°) gives 093° as the bearing of C from A.
questions.p: Since course change from 040° to 130°, the turn for B na 90° (right angle), so triangle ABC get right angle for B with legs 60 km and 80 km. The angle for A between AB and AC na arctan(80/60) = 53.13°. If you add am to bearing of B from A (040°), you go get 093° as bearing of C from A.

questions.q: Surveying, as used in geography and land studies, is best described as the science and art of ____.
o: classifying rocks and minerals found in an area
measuring distances only with a tape
determining the relative positions, distances, and directions of points on or near the earth's surface
drawing freehand maps without any measurement
questions.e: Surveying involves finding out how points on land relate to one another in terms of position, distance, and direction, so that accurate maps and plans can be made. It is not just measuring with a tape or drawing freehand.
questions.p: Surveying na science and art wey dem dey use find how points for land relate with each other for position, distance and direction. E pass just measuring with tape or free hand drawing.

questions.q: In a simple chain survey carried out by a class of SS2 students in Enugu, which instrument is mainly used to measure horizontal distances between survey stations?
questions.e: The chain (or tape) is the basic tool for measuring horizontal distances in chain surveying. The theodolite measures angles, the ranging pole helps in sighting a straight line, and the compass measures bearings, not distance.
questions.p: Chain or tape na the main tool wey dem dey use measure the ground distance for chain survey. Theodolite na for angle, ranging pole na for sight straight line, compass na for bearing, no be distance.

questions.q: During a field survey near Abeokuta, a student took the bearing of point B from point A and recorded it as 040°. What is the bearing of point A from point B (the back bearing)?
questions.e: The back bearing is found by adding 180° to the forward bearing when it is less than 180°. So 040° + 180° = 220°. This 220° is the bearing of A as seen from B.
questions.p: To find back bearing when the first bearing small pass 180°, you go add 180° to am. So 040° + 180° = 220°, na so you go take find bearing of A from B.

questions.q: A topographical map of a part of Kano State has a scale of 1:50,000. If the distance between two settlements on the map is 4 cm, what is the actual distance between them on the ground, in kilometres?
questions.e: Actual distance = map distance x scale = 4 cm x 50,000 = 200,000 cm. Converting to km: 200,000 cm ÷ 100,000 (since 1 km = 100,000 cm) = 2 km.
questions.p: Real distance = map distance x scale = 4cm x 50,000 = 200,000cm. If you convert am to km, 200,000 ÷ 100,000 = 2km, since 1km be 100,000cm.

questions.q: A cocoa farm in Ondo State is represented on a map of scale 1:25,000 as a rectangle measuring 6 cm by 4 cm. What is the actual area of the farm on the ground, in square kilometres?
questions.e: Actual length = 6 cm x 25,000 = 150,000 cm = 1.5 km. Actual width = 4 cm x 25,000 = 100,000 cm = 1 km. Area = 1.5 km x 1 km = 1.5 km^2.
questions.p: Real length = 6cm x 25,000 = 150,000cm = 1.5km. Real width = 4cm x 25,000 = 100,000cm = 1km. Area = 1.5km x 1km = 1.5 km^2.

questions.q: In Geographic Information System (GIS) studies taught in Nigerian secondary schools, the acronym GIS stands for ____.
questions.e: GIS means Geographic Information System, a computer-based tool used to capture, store, analyse, and display spatial (location-based) data such as maps of towns, roads, and rivers.
questions.p: GIS mean Geographic Information System, na computer tool wey dem dey use capture, store, analyse and show spatial data like map of towns, roads and rivers.

questions.q: Which surveying instrument is specifically designed to measure both horizontal and vertical angles accurately during land levelling and mapping exercises?
questions.e: The theodolite is built to measure both horizontal and vertical angles precisely, which is essential in detailed land surveys. The chain measures length, ranging poles mark alignment, and the compass gives direction only.
questions.p: Theodolite na the instrument wey dem make specially to measure horizontal and vertical angle well-well. Chain na for length, ranging pole na for alignment, compass na for direction only.

questions.q: A group of surveying students carried out a closed traverse survey of a plot of land with 5 sides in Jos. When they added up all the interior angles they measured in the field, they got 538°. Given that the correct sum of interior angles of a closed traverse with n sides should be (n-2) x 180°, what is the angular error in their survey?
questions.e: For n = 5 sides, the correct sum should be (5-2) x 180° = 540°. The students measured 538°, so the error = 540° - 538° = 2°, which must be distributed among the angles to correct the survey.
questions.p: For n = 5 sides, the correct total suppose be (5-2) x 180° = 540°. Dem measure 538°, so the error na 540° - 538° = 2°, wey dem go share am well among the angles to correct the survey.

questions.q: Approximately how long does it take the earth to complete one full rotation on its axis, which produces day and night?
questions.e: The earth rotates once on its axis in about 24 hours. This spinning motion is what causes day and night as different parts of the earth face or turn away from the sun.
questions.p: Earth dey do one complete turn for im axis for like 24 hours. Na dis turning dey cause day and night as different parts of earth dey face or comot from sun.

questions.q: The earth's revolution around the sun, combined with the tilt of its axis, mainly causes which of the following?
questions.e: As the earth moves round the sun in about 365 1/4 days, its tilted axis makes different parts of the earth receive more or less direct sunlight at different times of the year, giving rise to seasons.
questions.p: As earth dey waka round sun for like 365 1/4 days, the way im axis dey tilt make different part of earth receive sun well-well for different time, na so season dey change.

questions.q: Town A is located on longitude 15°E and Town B is located on longitude 45°W. If the local time at Town A is 12:00 noon, what is the local time at Town B?
questions.e: Total longitude difference = 15 + 45 = 60°. Since 15° equals 1 hour, 60° equals 4 hours. Town B is west of Town A, so its time is behind: 12:00 noon minus 4 hours = 8:00am.
questions.p: Total longitude wey dey between dem na 15+45=60°. Since 15° na 1 hour, 60° go be 4 hours. Town B dey west, so im time dey behind: 12noon minus 4hrs = 8am.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a line of latitude?
questions.e: Lines of latitude run parallel to the Equator and measure positions north or south. The Prime Meridian, however, is a line of longitude used to measure positions east or west, so it is not a latitude.
questions.p: Latitude lines dey run parallel to Equator, dem dey show north-south position. Prime Meridian na longitude line wey dey show east-west position, so e no be latitude.

questions.q: Lagos is located on longitude 3°E. Town X has a local time that is 2 hours ahead of Lagos' local time. What is the approximate longitude of Town X?
questions.e: A time difference of 2 hours equals 2 x 15° = 30° of longitude. Since Town X's time is ahead, it lies to the east of Lagos, so its longitude = 3°E + 30° = 33°E.
questions.p: Time wey different na 2hrs, e equal 2x15=30° longitude. Since Town X time dey ahead, e dey east of Lagos, so im longitude na 3°E+30°=33°E.

questions.q: The circumference of the earth at the equator is approximately 40,000 km, and the earth completes one full rotation in about 24 hours. What is the approximate linear speed of a point on the equator, in km/h?
questions.e: Speed = distance / time = 40000 km / 24 hours = 1666.67 km/h, which rounds to about 1667 km/h. This shows how fast points on the equator move as the earth spins.
questions.p: Speed = distance divide time = 40000km/24hours = 1666.67 km/h, wey round up go 1667 km/h. Na so fast point for equator dey move as earth dey spin.

questions.q: Greenwich Mean Time (GMT) is best described as what?
o: Local time at the Tropic of Cancer
Local time at the International Date Line
questions.e: GMT is the local time at the Prime Meridian, which is longitude 0°, passing through Greenwich in London. It is used as the reference point for calculating time differences across the world.
questions.p: GMT na the local time for Prime Meridian, wey be longitude 0°, wey dey pass through Greenwich London. Dem dey use am as reference to calculate time difference for other places.

questions.q: What is the maximum value that a line of latitude can have, measured from the Equator?
questions.e: Latitude is measured from 0° at the Equator to 90° at either the North Pole or the South Pole, so 90° is the highest possible latitude value.
questions.p: Dem dey measure latitude from 0° for Equator go reach 90° for North Pole or South Pole, so 90° na the highest value wey latitude fit be.

questions.q: Which of the following is the thin, solid, outermost layer of the earth on which human beings, plants and animals live?
questions.e: The crust is the thin, solid outer layer of the earth that forms the land surface and the ocean floor. It is much thinner than the mantle and core, which lie beneath it.
questions.p: Crust na di thin solid layer wey dey outside di earth wia we dey waka and build house. E dey thinner pass di mantle and core wey dey inside am.

questions.q: Rocks that are formed when molten magma from inside the earth cools and solidifies, either on the surface or below it, are called?
questions.e: Igneous rocks form directly from the cooling and hardening of magma or lava. Examples include granite (cools slowly underground) and basalt (cools quickly on the surface).
questions.p: Igneous rocks na rocks wey form when magma cool and hard, either under ground or for di surface. Example na granite and basalt.

questions.q: The continental crust, which is lighter in density and rich in silica and aluminium, is commonly referred to by geographers as?
questions.e: The continental crust is called Sial because it is made mainly of silica (Si) and aluminium (Al) compounds. It is lighter than the oceanic crust (Sima), which is rich in silica and magnesium.
questions.p: Dem dey call continental crust 'Sial' because e dey get plenty silica (Si) and aluminium (Al). E light pass oceanic crust (Sima) wey get silica and magnesium.

questions.q: Over many years, loose sand grains deposited by a river in the Niger Delta became compacted and cemented together by natural minerals to form a hard rock. This rock is best classified as?
questions.e: Sandstone is a sedimentary rock formed when loose sand grains are compacted and cemented together over long periods. Granite and basalt are igneous rocks, while marble is metamorphic.
questions.p: Sandstone na sedimentary rock wey form when sand particles squeeze and cement togeda for long time. Granite and basalt na igneous rock, marble na metamorphic rock.

questions.q: A block of limestone that is buried deep in the earth is subjected to intense heat and pressure over millions of years, changing its structure without melting it completely. The new rock formed is most likely to be?
questions.e: Marble is a metamorphic rock formed when limestone is changed by heat and pressure without fully melting. This process recrystallises the minerals in the limestone into marble.
questions.p: Marble na metamorphic rock wey form when limestone meet heat and pressure wey change am without melt am well well. Di minerals inside limestone go recrystallise come be marble.

questions.q: A geography student learns that the density of the earth's layers increases steadily from the surface towards the centre. Which sequence correctly arranges the earth's layers from the LEAST dense to the MOST dense?
o: Crust, Outer core, Inner core, Mantle
Mantle, Crust, Outer core, Inner core
Inner core, Outer core, Mantle, Crust
Crust, Mantle, Outer core, Inner core
questions.e: The crust is the lightest layer, followed by the mantle, then the outer core, with the inner core (mostly solid iron and nickel under extreme pressure) being the densest. Density increases steadily from the surface towards the centre of the earth.
questions.p: Crust na di lightest layer, den mantle, den outer core, and inner core (wey be solid iron and nickel wey pressure squeeze well well) na di heaviest. Density dey increase as e dey go inside towards di centre.

questions.q: A piece of marble (a metamorphic rock) is heated until it melts completely into magma, and the magma is then allowed to cool and solidify into a new rock. What type of rock will this new rock be classified as?
questions.e: Once a rock melts completely into magma, its original identity is destroyed. When this magma cools and solidifies, it always forms an igneous rock, regardless of what the rock was before melting.
questions.p: Once rock melt well well come be magma, e don lose im former identity. Wen dis magma cool come hard, na igneous rock e go become, no matter wetin di rock be before.

questions.q: Which of the following best defines a mineral as used in the study of rocks?
o: Any substance dug out of the ground for industrial use
A naturally occurring inorganic substance with a definite chemical composition and crystalline structure
A layer of the earth located below the crust
A rock formed from the cooling of magma
questions.e: A mineral is a naturally occurring, inorganic substance with a fixed chemical composition and an orderly crystal structure, such as quartz or mica. Rocks are usually made up of a combination of different minerals.
questions.p: Mineral na natural, inorganic substance wey get fixed chemical composition and crystal arrangement, like quartz or mica. Rocks na combination of different minerals.

questions.q: Folding of rock layers in the Earth's crust is mainly caused by which type of earth movement?
o: Horizontal compressive forces pushing rock layers together
Sudden release of volcanic gases underground
Surface erosion by rivers and wind over time
Vertical forces lifting a block of land upward only
questions.e: Folding happens when horizontal compressive forces squeeze rock layers, causing them to bend into upfolds (anticlines) and downfolds (synclines). Erosion and gas release do not fold rock layers.
questions.p: Na when force dey push rock layers from side to side dem go bend, dat one na folding. Erosion and gas no fit cause folding.

questions.q: Which instrument is specifically used by scientists to detect and record the strength (magnitude) of earthquake waves?
questions.e: A seismograph records the vibrations produced by earthquakes and is used to measure their magnitude. The other instruments measure pressure, wind speed, and humidity respectively, not earthquakes.
questions.p: Seismograph na di instrument wey dem dey use measure earthquake strength. Di oda ones na for pressure, wind and humidity, no be for earthquake.

questions.q: During faulting, a block of land that sinks down and lies lower than the surrounding land, bounded on both sides by parallel faults, is called a:
questions.e: A graben (also called a rift valley) is a depressed block of land that has sunk between two parallel faults. A horst is the opposite, a raised block, while anticline and syncline are fold features, not fault features.
questions.p: Graben na land wey sink down between two parallel fault lines, dem dey call am rift valley too. Horst na di opposite, na raised land, while anticline and syncline na for folding, no be fault.

questions.q: Which landform results from intrusive vulcanicity, where magma squeezes between two existing rock layers and solidifies there without ever reaching the Earth's surface?
questions.e: A sill is a sheet of solidified magma that forms when magma intrudes horizontally between existing rock layers and cools underground. Volcanic cones, calderas, and lava plateaus are all extrusive features formed on the surface.
questions.p: Sill na when magma enter between rock layers under ground and cool there, e no reach surface. Volcanic cone, caldera and lava plateau na extrusive features wey dey show for surface.

questions.q: An upward fold (ridge-shaped bend) of rock strata, where the oldest rock layers are exposed at the core after erosion has stripped away the younger layers, is known as a/an:
questions.e: An anticline is an upfold where rock layers arch upward, and once eroded, the oldest rocks are exposed at its centre. A syncline is a downfold, while horst and rift valley relate to faulting, not folding.
questions.p: Anticline na upfold wey rock arch go up, and after erosion, di oldest rock go dey center. Syncline na downfold, while horst and rift valley na for faulting matter.

questions.q: Geographers sometimes find that in a folded landscape, the highest hills actually sit where the original synclines (troughs) were, while the original anticlines (crests) form valleys. What best explains this relief inversion?
o: Anticlines contain denser rock that sinks over time, turning them into valleys
The crest of an anticline is stretched and cracked by tension, making it erode faster than the compressed rock of the syncline
Rivers naturally flow uphill from anticlines into nearby synclines
Synclines are always made of volcanic rock that cannot be worn away
questions.e: At the crest of an anticline, rock layers are stretched and develop cracks, which weakens them and makes them erode more easily than the compressed, less-fractured rock in the syncline trough. Over long periods, this can reverse the original relief so synclines become hills and anticlines become valleys.
questions.p: For anticline crest, di rock dey stretch and crack, dis one dey make am weak and e dey erode fast pass di rock for syncline wey dem press together. As time dey go, dis fit turn di hill to valley and di valley to hill, na so relief inversion dey happen.

questions.q: A seismograph station recorded that the primary (P) waves of an earthquake arrived 4 minutes before the secondary (S) waves. If the P-wave travels at 8 km per second and the S-wave travels at 4 km per second, calculate the distance of the station from the earthquake's epicentre.
questions.e: Convert 4 minutes to seconds: 4 x 60 = 240 s. Using distance = (Vp x Vs / (Vp - Vs)) x time difference = (8x4/(8-4)) x 240 = 8 x 240 = 1920 km. This formula accounts for the fact that the faster P-wave pulls ahead of the S-wave as distance increases.
questions.p: Change 4 minutes to seconds: 4 x 60 = 240 s. Use di formula distance = (Vp x Vs divide by (Vp - Vs)) x time wey dem take reach = (8x4/(8-4)) x 240 = 8 x 240 = 1920 km. Dis formula show say di faster P-wave go dey front pass di S-wave as distance dey increase.

questions.q: Which type of volcano has a low, broad, gently sloping profile because it is built up from highly fluid lava that flows easily over long distances before solidifying?
questions.e: A shield volcano is formed from very fluid basaltic lava that spreads out widely before cooling, giving it a broad, gentle, dome-like shape similar to a warrior's shield. Composite volcanoes have steeper sides from alternating ash and lava, cinder cones are steep and made of loose fragments, and a caldera is a collapsed crater, not a volcano type built by flowing lava.
questions.p: Shield volcano dey form from very watery lava wey dey spread far before e cool down, so e dey broad and flat like shield. Composite volcano get steep side from ash and lava mix, cinder cone na loose fragments wey steep, and caldera na collapsed crater, e no be type of volcano wey lava flow build.

questions.q: What is the best definition of weathering as used in Geography?
o: The wearing away and transportation of rock particles by moving water or wind
The movement of broken rock materials down a slope under gravity
The laying down of sediments carried by rivers, wind or ice
The breakdown and decay of rocks in their original position without being transported
questions.e: Weathering is the in-situ (on the spot) breakdown of rocks by mechanical, chemical or biological processes. It does not involve movement of the broken material, which is handled by erosion or mass movement.
questions.p: Weathering na when rock dey break or spoil for the same place wey e dey, no movement involved. If material move go another place, na erosion or mass movement be dat.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of mechanical (physical) weathering?
o: Frost shattering of rocks in cold climates
questions.e: Frost shattering happens when water in rock cracks freezes, expands, and splits the rock apart physically, with no change in chemical composition. Carbonation, hydrolysis and oxidation are all chemical weathering processes.
questions.p: Frost shattering na physical process, water enter rock crack, freeze, expand, e burst the rock, no chemical change dey happen. Carbonation, hydrolysis and oxidation na chemical weathering.

questions.q: In the Sahel region of West Africa, large daily temperature swings cause rock surfaces to expand by day and contract by night until outer layers peel off like onion skin. This process is called...
questions.e: Exfoliation, also called insolation weathering, occurs where large daily temperature range makes rock surfaces expand and contract repeatedly, causing outer layers to peel off in sheets. This is common in hot desert and semi-desert areas like the Sahel.
questions.p: Exfoliation na when the hot sun for daytime and cold for night make rock dey expand and shrink well-well, until the outside layer peel comot like onion. E dey happen well for desert and Sahel area.

questions.q: Which chemical weathering process involves rainwater containing dissolved carbon dioxide reacting with rocks such as limestone, dissolving them over time?
questions.e: Carbonation occurs when rainwater absorbs carbon dioxide from the air to form weak carbonic acid, which reacts with calcium carbonate in limestone, dissolving it. This is why limestone areas often have caves and sinkholes.
questions.p: Carbonation na when rain water carry CO2 form weak acid, e react with limestone (calcium carbonate) make am melt small small. Na why limestone area dey get cave and sinkhole.

questions.q: Which type of mass movement is best described as the very slow, almost unnoticeable downslope shifting of soil particles over months or years?
questions.e: Soil creep is the slowest type of mass movement, where soil particles move downslope so gradually that it cannot be observed directly, though evidence like tilted fences or bent tree trunks shows it over time. Landslide, rockfall and mudflow are all much faster movements.
questions.p: Soil creep na the slowest mass movement, soil dey move small small for long time, you no fit see am with eye but fence wey bend or tree wey tilt fit show say e don happen. Landslide, rockfall and mudflow dey faster pass am.

questions.q: A farmer on the Jos Plateau notices that tree roots growing into cracks in a large granite boulder have gradually widened the cracks until the rock split into separate blocks. This process is best described as...
questions.e: When living organisms such as plant roots or burrowing animals cause rocks to break apart, it is called biological weathering. Frost action needs freezing temperatures which are rare on the Jos Plateau, and hydrolysis is a chemical reaction, not root growth.
questions.p: When plant root or animal dey cause rock to break, na biological weathering. Frost action need very cold temperature wey no dey common for Jos Plateau, and hydrolysis na chemical reaction, e no concern root growth.

questions.q: Which combination of climatic conditions would most speed up chemical weathering of rocks in a tropical rainforest area such as parts of southern Nigeria?
o: High altitude and strong dry winds
Low humidity and high wind speed
questions.e: Chemical weathering reactions such as hydrolysis and carbonation speed up with more heat and more moisture, since both heat and water encourage chemical reactions in rock minerals. Tropical rainforest areas have high temperature and heavy rainfall, making chemical weathering very active there compared to dry or cold regions.
questions.p: Chemical weathering dey faster when heat and water plenty, because heat and moisture dey push chemical reaction for inside rock. Tropical rainforest get plenty heat and rain, so chemical weathering dey strong pass dry or cold area.

questions.q: During heavy rainfall near Enugu, a thick layer of saturated soil and loose rock debris on a steep slope suddenly moves rapidly downhill as a fast-flowing watery mass, destroying a farm at the base of the slope. This type of mass movement is best classified as...
questions.e: A mudflow is a rapid, water-saturated flow of soil and debris down a slope, usually triggered by heavy rain, and it moves much faster than soil creep. Solifluction is slow movement in cold, frozen-ground regions, and rockfall is the sudden drop of rock from a cliff, not a flowing watery mass.
questions.p: Mudflow na fast movement of soil and debris wey water don soak well-well, e dey happen quick quick after heavy rain, e no be like soil creep wey slow. Solifluction dey happen for cold frozen ground, and rockfall na when rock just fall from cliff straight, no flowing water involved.

questions.q: A river meander develops such a tight loop that the narrow neck of land between the two bends is eventually eroded through during a flood. The river then takes the shorter, straighter path, and the abandoned loop is sealed off from the main channel, forming a crescent-shaped lake beside the river. What is this crescent-shaped lake called?
questions.e: When a meander neck is cut through, the old loop is separated from the main flow and remains as a curved, crescent-shaped lake. This feature is called an oxbow lake. It is a classic landform of the middle to lower course of a river.
questions.p: When river cut through the narrow neck of one big bend, the old bend go turn to separate curve-shaped lake wey dem dey call oxbow lake. Na common feature for where river dey meander well-well. E no be delta, floodplain or waterfall.

questions.q: In the upper (youthful) course of a river, the river mostly cuts straight down into the land rather than sideways, because its energy is used mainly for vertical erosion over a steep gradient. Which landform is typically produced by this process?
questions.e: In the youthful stage, a river has high energy and a steep slope, so it erodes downward quickly, cutting a narrow, steep-sided valley shaped like the letter V. Deltas, floodplains and levees belong to the middle or lower course where lateral erosion and deposition dominate.
questions.p: For the upper part of river (young stage), the river dey cut down straight (vertical erosion) because of steep slope and plenty energy, so e go form narrow valley wey resemble letter V. Delta, floodplain and levee na for middle/lower course where deposition dey happen.

questions.q: A river flows across land where a layer of hard, resistant rock lies on top of a layer of soft, less resistant rock, both lying roughly horizontal across the river's path. Over time, the soft rock beneath is worn away faster by the flowing water, undercutting the hard rock layer above it until it collapses, and the process repeats as the river retreats upstream. Which landform does this process best explain?
questions.e: Differential erosion of hard rock over soft rock causes undercutting and periodic collapse of the hard rock ledge, creating a sudden vertical drop in the river's course. This is exactly how a waterfall (with a plunge pool) forms and migrates upstream over time.
questions.p: Because soft rock dey wear away fast pass the hard rock wey dey on top am, the hard rock go dey hang until e break/collapse, and this process go continue to happen as river dey move backward. Na so waterfall dey form, no be delta, floodplain or meander.

questions.q: As a river flows around a bend in its middle course, the water flows fastest on the outer side of the bend, causing erosion there, while it flows slowest on the inner side, allowing sand and silt to be deposited there forming a point bar. Over many years this process makes the river channel develop a winding, snake-like shape. What is this winding shape of the channel called?
questions.e: Faster current on the outer bank erodes it, while slower current on the inner bank deposits sediment as a point bar; repeating this on successive bends produces a winding, snake-like channel pattern called a meander. A gorge, levee and braided channel are different landforms formed by different processes.
questions.p: Fast water for outside bend dey erode am, slow water for inside bend dey drop sand (point bar); if this dey happen for many bends, the river go bend-bend like snake. Na so meander dey form, e no be gorge, levee or braided channel.

questions.q: A river carrying a heavy load of sediment enters a calm sea with weak tides and currents, so that it can no longer carry all its load. The sediment drops and builds up at the river's mouth, sometimes splitting the river into several smaller channels called distributaries. Which landform is formed as a result?
questions.e: When a sediment-laden river meets calm water with weak currents, it deposits its load at its mouth instead of carrying it further, building up a low, fan-shaped or triangular landform often crossed by distributaries. This landform is called a delta, as seen at the mouth of the River Niger.
questions.p: When river wey carry plenty sediment enter calm sea wey no get strong current, e go drop the sediment for the mouth, sometimes e go divide to small channels (distributaries). Na so delta dey form, like River Niger delta.

questions.q: Due to a fall in sea level, a river that had previously been flowing sluggishly across a wide floodplain starts to cut downward again into its own former floodplain. This leaves flat, step-like platforms of the old floodplain standing on both sides of the new, deeper valley, well above the current river level. What term best describes these raised, flat platforms?
questions.e: A fall in sea level (or land uplift) lowers the river's base level, causing renewed downward erosion (rejuvenation) into its old floodplain. The remnants of the old floodplain left standing above the new, narrower valley are called river terraces. Deltas, levees and potholes are unrelated features formed by different processes.
questions.p: When sea level fall, the river go get new energy to cut down again inside im old floodplain (rejuvenation). The leftover flat parts of the old floodplain wey remain for both sides, up high pass the new river level, na river terraces. E no be delta, levee or pothole.

questions.q: River A has a steeper gradient and greater erosive power than its neighbour, River B, which shares a common watershed (divide) with it. Over a long period, River A erodes headward through the watershed until it breaks into the upper valley of River B, diverting River B's headwaters into River A's channel. Downstream of this point, River B's original valley is left dry or carries only a small stream. What is this process called?
questions.e: A river with a steeper gradient erodes headward faster and can break through the watershed into a neighbouring river's valley, diverting its headwaters; this is called river capture or drainage piracy. The captured river's former course beyond the capture point is left as a dry or under-fit valley called a wind gap.
questions.p: Because River A get steeper slope, e get more power to cut backward (headward erosion) until e break enter River B valley and carry B headwaters comot. Na so dem dey call river capture (drainage piracy); the dry valley wey remain na wind gap.

questions.q: During repeated flooding, a river overflows its banks and the fastest-flowing, coarser sediment settles close to the channel edges while finer material spreads further onto the floodplain. Over many floods this builds up raised, ridge-like banks running along both sides of the river channel. What are these raised ridges called?
questions.e: Repeated flooding deposits coarse sediment nearer the channel (because the river loses energy quickly once it leaves the channel), building raised ridges along the banks called levees. Potholes, gorges and oxbow lakes are formed by erosion or channel-cutting processes, not by this kind of flood deposition.
questions.p: Anytime river flood, the coarse sediment dey settle near the bank while fine sediment dey spread far; if this dey repeat, e go build raised ridge for both sides of the channel wey dem call levees. Pothole, gorge and oxbow lake no be the same thing with levee.

questions.q: Which of these desert landforms is produced mainly by WIND DEPOSITION, forming a crescent-shaped mound of sand whose 'horns' point in the direction the wind is blowing?
questions.e: A barchan is a crescent-shaped sand dune built up by wind deposition where sand supply is limited and wind direction is fairly constant. Zeugen and yardang are erosional features carved by wind, while a cirque is a glacial landform, not a wind feature.
questions.p: Barchan na sand hill wey wind dey deposit, e dey look like crescent moon, and e horns dey point to where wind dey blow go. Zeugen and yardang na erosion landform wey wind carve, cirque na glacier landform.

questions.q: In a desert region, wind-blown sand wears away softer rock faster than harder rock where the rock bands lie VERTICALLY, roughly parallel to the direction of the prevailing wind. This leaves long, streamlined, ridge-like masses of rock aligned with the wind. What is this landform called?
questions.e: A yardang is a streamlined, ridge-shaped rock mass formed when wind erosion acts on rock bands that run parallel to the wind direction. Zeugen instead form from horizontally layered rock, and mushroom rocks result from stronger erosion near the base.
questions.p: Yardang na long rock ridge wey wind carve where the rock layers dey stand straight, dey follow the wind direction. Zeugen na from rock wey dey lie flat, mushroom rock na from strong erosion for the rock bottom.

questions.q: On a mountainside, ice collects in a hollow and through freeze-thaw weathering and plucking at the back wall, a deep, armchair-shaped basin is carved out, often with a rock lip at its open end that may later hold a small lake. What is this glacial landform called?
questions.e: A cirque (also called a corrie) is a bowl-shaped hollow carved by glacial ice through plucking and freeze-thaw action, usually with a rock lip at the front. A fjord is a flooded glacial valley, an arete is a sharp ridge, and a drumlin is a depositional mound.
questions.p: Cirque na the bowl-shape hollow wey ice dey carve for mountain side through plucking and freeze-thaw. Fjord na glacier valley wey water don enter, arete na sharp ridge, drumlin na small hill wey ice deposit leave.

questions.q: Along a coastline, longshore drift carries sand past a bend in the shore and deposits it in open water, building a narrow ridge of sand that is attached to the land at one end but has a free, often hooked, end projecting into the sea. What is this coastal landform called?
questions.e: A spit is a narrow ridge of sand or shingle attached to the coast at one end, built by longshore drift depositing material beyond a change in coastline direction. A bar joins two headlands fully across a bay, a tombolo joins the mainland to an island, and a lagoon is the water body often trapped behind such features.
questions.p: Spit na long sand ridge wey dey attach to land for one side, but the other side dey free, dey enter sea; longshore drift build am. Bar dey join two headland fully, tombolo dey join mainland to island, lagoon na water wey dey trap behind these features.

questions.q: A long, narrow, very deep inlet of the sea, bordered by steep rocky cliffs, is formed when a glacier that had carved a deep U-shaped valley all the way to the coast melts away and the sea later rises to flood the lower part of that valley. What is this coastal landform called?
questions.e: A fjord forms when a glacially-carved U-shaped valley is flooded by the sea, giving steep sides and great depth. A ria is a flooded river valley (V-shaped, not glacial), an estuary is a tidal river mouth, and a delta is built from river sediment deposition.
questions.p: Fjord na when sea water enter the U-shape valley wey glacier don carve, e get steep side and e deep well well. Ria na flooded river valley (V-shape), estuary na river mouth wey tide dey enter, delta na where river deposit sediment.

questions.q: At a point along the Nigerian coastline, waves keep pushing sand toward a small offshore island until the sand ridge finally grows long enough to join the island permanently to the mainland. What is the resulting landform called?
questions.e: A tombolo is a sand or shingle ridge formed by wave deposition that links an offshore island to the mainland. A spit has a free end not attached to another landmass, a bay bar seals off a whole bay, and a barrier beach lies parallel offshore without necessarily joining an island.
questions.p: Tombolo na sand ridge wey waves build wey join island to mainland well well. Spit get free end wey no join any island, bay bar dey close whole bay, barrier beach dey lie for offshore without joining island.

questions.q: In a desert area, hard and soft rock occur in alternating bands lying HORIZONTALLY (parallel to the ground surface). Over time, wind-blown sand wears away the softer rock faster than the harder rock, leaving flat-topped blocks of hard rock standing on narrower pedestals of the remaining softer rock. What is this landform called?
questions.e: Zeugen form where horizontal layers of hard and soft rock are unevenly eroded by wind, leaving table-like hard rock blocks on thinner soft-rock bases. Yardangs instead come from vertically aligned rock bands parallel to wind direction, barchans are depositional dunes, and inselbergs are isolated hills left after extensive weathering, not specifically a wind-erosion feature.
questions.p: Zeugen dey form where hard and soft rock dey lie flat for ground, wind go wear the soft one pass the hard one, leave table-like hard rock for top thin soft-rock base. Yardang na from rock wey stand straight dey follow wind, barchan na deposited sand hill, inselberg na lone hill wey weathering leave.

questions.q: As a glacier advances down a valley and then stops advancing, it drops the rocky debris it has been carrying right at its farthest point reached, building a ridge that marks the maximum extent of the ice before it began to retreat. What is this depositional landform called?
questions.e: A terminal moraine is the ridge of debris deposited at the farthest point reached by a glacier, marking its maximum advance. A lateral moraine forms along the valley sides, a medial moraine forms where two glaciers merge, and ground moraine is debris spread beneath the ice over the valley floor.
questions.p: Terminal moraine na the ridge of debris wey glacier drop for the farthest point e reach before e start to comot. Lateral moraine dey form for valley side, medial moraine dey form where two glacier join, ground moraine na debris wey spread for valley floor under the ice.

questions.q: Which instrument is used to measure atmospheric pressure?
questions.e: A barometer measures the pressure of the atmosphere, which helps forecast weather changes. The anemometer measures wind speed, the hygrometer measures humidity, and the rain gauge measures rainfall.
questions.p: Barometer na the instrument wey dem dey use measure air pressure. Anemometer na for wind speed, hygrometer na for humidity, rain gauge na for rainfall.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT an element of weather but rather a factor that influences climate?
questions.e: Temperature, humidity and rainfall are elements of weather that can be measured day to day. Latitude is a factor that controls climate (through sunlight and temperature patterns) but is not itself a weather element.
questions.p: Temperature, humidity and rainfall na weather elements wey you fit measure every day. Latitude na factor wey dey affect climate, e no be weather element.

questions.q: Which instrument is used to determine the direction from which the wind is blowing?
questions.e: The wind vane has an arrow that turns to point in the direction the wind is coming from. The anemometer measures wind speed, not direction, while the barometer and hygrometer measure pressure and humidity respectively.
questions.p: Wind vane get arrow wey dey turn show where wind dey come from. Anemometer na for wind speed, barometer na for pressure, hygrometer na for humidity.

questions.q: On a certain day in Kano, the maximum temperature recorded was 36°C while the minimum temperature was 22°C. What is the diurnal (daily) temperature range for that day?
questions.e: Diurnal temperature range is found by subtracting the minimum temperature from the maximum temperature: 36°C minus 22°C equals 14°C. This tells us how much the temperature varied within that single day.
questions.p: To find daily range, you minus minimum temperature from maximum: 36°C minus 22°C na 14°C. Na so you go know how temperature change within that day.

questions.q: The mean monthly temperature of the hottest month in a town is 34°C, while that of the coldest month is 26°C. Calculate the annual temperature range of the town.
questions.e: Annual temperature range is the difference between the hottest month's mean temperature and the coldest month's mean temperature: 34°C minus 26°C equals 8°C.
questions.p: Annual temperature range na difference between the hottest month temperature and the coldest month temperature: 34°C minus 26°C na 8°C.

questions.q: The temperature of a town was recorded four times in a day as follows: 6am = 18°C, 12noon = 32°C, 6pm = 28°C, 12midnight = 14°C. Calculate the mean daily temperature for that town.
questions.e: To find the mean, add all four readings together and divide by the number of readings: (18+32+28+14) = 92, and 92 divided by 4 equals 23°C.
questions.p: To find the mean, add all the four readings together: (18+32+28+14) = 92, then divide am by 4, you go get 23°C.

questions.q: At a certain height in the atmosphere, the air contains 9 grammes of water vapour per kilogram of air, while the maximum amount of water vapour the air could hold at that same temperature is 12 grammes per kilogram. Calculate the relative humidity of the air at that point.
questions.e: Relative humidity is calculated as the actual water vapour content divided by the maximum possible water vapour content, multiplied by 100: (9/12) x 100 equals 75%. This shows the air is holding 75% of the moisture it could possibly hold at that temperature.
questions.p: Relative humidity na the actual water vapour wey dey air divide by the maximum e fit hold, times 100: (9/12) x 100 na 75%. Na so e show say the air don carry 75% of the water e fit hold.

questions.q: The total rainfall recorded at a weather station for the months of June, July and August were 180mm, 210mm and 150mm respectively. Calculate the mean monthly rainfall for these three months.
questions.e: To find the mean monthly rainfall, add the three monthly totals and divide by 3: (180+210+150) = 540, and 540 divided by 3 equals 180mm. Note that 540mm is only the total, not the mean, which is a common mistake candidates should avoid.
questions.p: To find the mean monthly rainfall, add the three months totals: (180+210+150) = 540, then divide am by 3, you go get 180mm. Make you no mistake 540mm as the answer, na only the total, e no be the mean.

questions.q: Which scientist developed the most widely used system of classifying world climates, based mainly on temperature and precipitation patterns?
questions.e: Wladimir Koppen, a German climatologist, developed the most widely used climate classification system. He grouped climates using temperature and rainfall data together with vegetation patterns.
questions.p: Wladimir Koppen na the German climatologist wey develop di classification wey pipo dey use pass. E use temperature and rainfall data plus vegetation to group di climates.

questions.q: Which of the following is a typical feature of the equatorial climate type, found in areas like the Niger Delta region of Nigeria?
o: A large diurnal temperature range of more than 20°C
A single short rainy season followed by a long dry season
Annual rainfall below 250mm with a very dry atmosphere
Two rainfall maxima in a year with no distinct dry season
questions.e: The equatorial climate has two rainfall peaks (around the equinoxes) because the sun is overhead twice a year, giving heavy rainfall almost all year with no long dry season. This differs from savanna and desert climates.
questions.p: Equatorial climate get two rain peak for di year because sun dey overhead twice, so rain dey fall almost di whole year without long dry season. Na dis one different am from savanna and desert climate.

questions.q: The tropical continental climate (Sudan type) found in northern Nigeria, around towns like Kano and Sokoto, is best described by which of the following?
o: Rainfall exceeds 2000mm annually with high humidity all year
Temperature remains constant throughout the year with little seasonal change
A single wet season occurs during the high-sun period, followed by a long dry season
Rainfall occurs throughout the year with no dry season
questions.e: The Sudan (tropical continental) climate has one rainy season linked to the overhead sun and the moist monsoon wind, followed by a long dry season dominated by the dry Harmattan wind from the Sahara. This gives it a clear wet and dry seasonal pattern, unlike the equatorial type.
questions.p: Sudan (tropical continental) climate get one rainy season wey dey follow when sun dey overhead and moist wind dey blow, then long dry season follow am wen Harmattan dey blow from Sahara. So di climate get clear wet and dry season, unlike equatorial type.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes the Mediterranean climate type?
o: Warm dry summers and mild wet winters
Uniform rainfall throughout the year with moderate temperature
Hot wet summers and cool dry winters
Cold wet summers and hot dry winters
questions.e: The Mediterranean climate is marked by warm, dry summers (because subtropical high pressure dominates) and mild, wet winters (because westerly winds and depressions bring rain). This seasonal reversal of rainfall is its key identifying feature.
questions.p: Mediterranean climate get warm dry summer (because subtropical high pressure dey control am) and mild wet winter (because westerly wind and depression dey bring rain). Na dis change of rain pattern be im main identity.

questions.q: A meteorological station in northern Nigeria recorded a mean monthly temperature of 18°C in its coolest month (January) and 32°C in its hottest month (May, before the rains). Calculate the annual temperature range of this station.
questions.e: Annual temperature range = highest mean monthly temperature minus lowest mean monthly temperature = 32°C - 18°C = 14°C. A range this size is common in tropical continental (Sudan) climates away from the coast, unlike the small range seen in equatorial coastal areas.
questions.p: Annual temperature range = di highest mean monthly temperature minus di lowest one = 32°C - 18°C = 14°C. Dis kain big range dey common for tropical continental (Sudan) climate wey far from coast, unlike small range wey dey equatorial coastal area.

questions.q: Which of the following best distinguishes the tropical monsoon climate from the equatorial climate?
o: Monsoon climate occurs only at the poles while equatorial climate occurs at the equator
Equatorial climate has four distinct seasons while monsoon climate has only one season
Monsoon climate has a short dry season caused by seasonal reversal of wind direction, while equatorial climate has rainfall spread fairly evenly all year
Monsoon climate has lower total annual rainfall than equatorial climate
questions.e: Monsoon climates (like in parts of Asia) experience a reversal of wind direction between seasons, giving a short but clear dry season alongside very heavy monsoon rains. Equatorial climates lack this wind reversal, so rainfall is heavy and fairly even throughout the year without a marked dry spell.
questions.p: Monsoon climate (like for some parts of Asia) get wind wey dey change direction between seasons, so e get short but clear dry season plus heavy monsoon rain. Equatorial climate no get dis wind change, so rain dey heavy and even throughout di year without clear dry period.

questions.q: Hot desert climates, such as that of the Sahara, typically have a very large diurnal (daily) temperature range compared to equatorial climates. Which of the following best explains this?
o: Deserts receive more rainfall than equatorial regions, increasing humidity and temperature range
Deserts are located at high altitudes where temperature is always low
Desert areas have thick cloud cover that traps heat at night
Clear skies and lack of vegetation in deserts allow rapid heat loss at night and rapid heating by day
questions.e: Deserts have clear skies and very little cloud or vegetation, so there is nothing to trap heat at night, causing temperatures to fall sharply, while intense direct sunlight during the day heats the bare ground quickly. This gives a large daily (diurnal) temperature range, unlike cloudy, humid equatorial areas where heat is retained at night.
questions.p: Desert get clear sky and almost no cloud or plant, so nothing dey trap heat for night, e dey make temperature drop sharply, while strong sun for daytime dey heat di bare ground quick quick. Na so e dey give big daily (diurnal) range, unlike cloudy humid equatorial area wey heat dey stay for night.

questions.q: In the Koppen system of climate classification, climate types are mainly grouped based on which two factors?
o: Ocean currents and wind direction alone
questions.e: Koppen's system classifies world climates mainly by comparing mean monthly and annual temperature with the amount and seasonal distribution of precipitation. These two factors determine the major climate groups such as equatorial, arid, warm temperate, and polar.
questions.p: Koppen system dey classify world climate mainly by comparing mean monthly and annual temperature with how much rain dey fall and wen e dey fall. Na dis two factors dey determine di main climate groups like equatorial, arid, warm temperate, and polar.

questions.q: Which of the following vegetation types is found in regions near the equator that receive heavy rainfall of over 2000mm annually, with high temperatures throughout the year, and is characterized by tall trees forming a continuous canopy with little undergrowth?
questions.e: Tropical rainforest grows in equatorial areas with heavy, well-distributed rainfall and constant high temperature, producing tall trees and a thick canopy. Savanna, temperate grassland and tundra occur in drier or colder climates that cannot support this type of forest.
questions.p: Tropical rainforest dey grow for equator area wey get plenty rain pass 2000mm every year and hot weather throughout. Na why e get tall trees wey form thick canopy. Savanna, temperate grass and tundra no get dis kain climate.

questions.q: In soil science, the process by which plant nutrients and minerals are washed down from the topsoil to the lower soil layers by heavy, continuous rainfall is called ______.
questions.e: Leaching is the downward movement of soluble nutrients through the soil caused by heavy rainfall, common in tropical areas. Weathering breaks down rocks, erosion removes soil from the surface, and evaporation is loss of water, not nutrient movement.
questions.p: Leaching na when heavy rain wash plant food (nutrients) comot from top soil go down. Weathering na when rock dey break, erosion na when soil dey carry comot from surface, and evaporation na water wey dey comot as vapour.

questions.q: Laterite soils, which are common in most parts of tropical Nigeria, are mainly formed as a result of which of the following processes?
o: Freezing and thawing of the soil surface
Accumulation of calcium carbonate due to low rainfall
Intense leaching under high rainfall and temperature, leaving behind iron and aluminium oxides
questions.e: In the tropics, heavy rainfall and high temperature cause intense leaching that removes soluble minerals, leaving behind insoluble iron and aluminium oxides that give laterite its reddish colour. Calcium carbonate build-up and freeze-thaw are features of dry and cold climates, not the humid tropics.
questions.p: For tropics, heavy rain and hot weather dey wash away soluble minerals, leave only iron and aluminium oxide wey make laterite red. Calcium carbonate dey build up for dry area, freeze-thaw na for cold area, no be tropics.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes the savanna (tropical grassland) vegetation belt found in the middle belt of Nigeria?
o: Evergreen trees with dense canopy and no grass cover
Short grasses and mosses with no trees due to permafrost
Cacti and succulent plants adapted to less than 250mm annual rainfall
Tall grasses with scattered drought-resistant trees, adapted to a distinct wet and dry season
questions.e: Savanna has tall grasses and widely spaced trees that can survive the long dry season, reflecting the alternating wet and dry seasons of the middle belt. Evergreen dense forest, permafrost tundra and desert cacti belong to completely different climatic zones.
questions.p: Savanna get tall grass and small-small trees wey fit survive long dry season, because the area get clear wet and dry season. Evergreen forest, tundra and desert cacti na for different climate entirely.

questions.q: A mature soil profile is divided into layers called horizons. Which horizon, usually darkest in colour, contains the highest amount of organic matter (humus) and is the layer from which minerals are leached downward?
questions.e: The A horizon is the topsoil, rich in humus from decayed plants and animals, giving it a dark colour, and it is where leaching of minerals begins. The B horizon receives the leached minerals, the C horizon is only partly weathered rock, and bedrock is unweathered solid rock.
questions.p: A horizon na the topsoil wey get plenty humus from dead plant and animal, so e dark in colour, and na from here minerals dey leach go down. B horizon na where the minerals land, C horizon na half-weathered rock, bedrock na solid rock wey never weather.

questions.q: Temperate deciduous forests, found in regions such as Western Europe, shed their leaves at a particular time of year. What is the main reason trees in this vegetation belt lose their leaves annually?
o: Because of excessive annual rainfall above 3000mm
To prevent attack by desert locusts
To reduce water loss and conserve energy during the cold winter months
questions.e: In winter, the ground water often freezes, making it hard for roots to absorb water, so trees shed their leaves to reduce transpiration and save energy until warmer, wetter conditions return in spring. Photosynthesis actually reduces in winter, locusts are not a factor in temperate Europe, and rainfall there is moderate, not excessive.
questions.p: For winter, water for ground dey freeze so the roots no fit drink water well, dat na why the trees dey comot their leaves to reduce water loss and save energy till spring come. Photosynthesis dey reduce for winter, locust no be di issue for Europe, and rain there no too plenty reach 3000mm.

questions.q: Desert soils, such as those found in the Sahara, usually accumulate calcium carbonate near the surface instead of the minerals being leached away. Which climatic condition is mainly responsible for this?
o: Low rainfall and high evaporation rate
questions.e: In deserts, rainfall is very low and evaporation is very high, so water rising to the surface carries dissolved calcium carbonate which is then deposited near the top instead of being washed deep down. Heavy rainfall, snow cover and high humidity would instead encourage leaching, not accumulation.
questions.p: For desert, rain no too dey and evaporation too high, so water wey dey rise go surface dey carry calcium carbonate wey e dey drop near top instead of e wash am go deep down. Heavy rain, snow or high humidity for suppose cause leaching, no be accumulation.

questions.q: Mediterranean vegetation, found around the Mediterranean Sea and parts of South Africa, must survive hot dry summers and mild wet winters. Which plant feature best helps these plants cope with the dry summer season?
o: Small, thick, waxy leaves that reduce transpiration
Broad thin leaves that maximize transpiration
Shallow roots that spread only on the soil surface
questions.e: Mediterranean plants are sclerophyllous, having small, thick, waxy leaves that cut down water loss through transpiration during the long dry summer. Broad thin leaves would increase water loss, shallow surface roots would dry out quickly, and plants cannot survive without roots at all.
questions.p: Mediterranean plants get small, thick, waxy leaves wey dey reduce how much water dey comot as transpiration during the long dry summer. Broad thin leaves go cause more water loss, shallow roots for surface go quick dry, and no plant fit survive without root at all.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a renewable natural resource?
questions.e: Renewable resources can be replenished naturally within a short time. Solar energy comes continuously from the sun and never runs out, unlike coal, crude oil and natural gas which take millions of years to form.
questions.p: Renewable resource na di one wey fit come back quick quick by itself. Solar energy dey come from sun anytime, but coal, crude oil and natural gas na fossil fuel wey need plenty years to form.

questions.q: The deliberate planting of trees on land that previously had no forest cover, mainly to combat desert encroachment, is called?
questions.e: Afforestation means planting trees in an area that did not have forest before. Reforestation, on the other hand, means replanting trees in an area where forest existed before but was cleared.
questions.p: Afforestation na when dem plant tree for land wey never get forest before. Reforestation na when dem replant tree for place wey forest dey before but dem don clear am.

questions.q: Which human activity is most directly responsible for accelerating desertification in the Sahel region of northern Nigeria?
questions.e: Overgrazing strips the land of its protective grass cover, leaving the soil bare and exposed to wind erosion. This weakens the soil's ability to hold moisture and speeds up the southward spread of desert conditions in the Sahel.
questions.p: When animal dem dey overgraze, dem dey finish all di grass wey dey cover ground. E go make soil naked and wind go easily blow am comot, so desert go dey spread fast for Sahel area.

questions.q: A natural hazard caused by a sudden release of energy within the earth's crust, resulting in shaking of the ground, is known as?
questions.e: An earthquake happens when stored energy along faults in the earth's crust is suddenly released, causing the ground to shake. A tsunami may result from an earthquake under the sea but is a different, secondary hazard.
questions.p: Earthquake na when energy wey dey hide inside earth crust burst comot suddenly, e go make ground shake. Tsunami fit happen after earthquake wey occur for sea, but na different hazard from earthquake.

questions.q: Which Nigerian state in the southeast is most noted for severe gully erosion problems caused by its loose, sandy soil and heavy rainfall?
questions.e: Anambra State sits on soft, sandy, poorly consolidated soil and receives heavy rainfall typical of southeastern Nigeria, making it very prone to deep gully erosion. Sokoto, Borno and Bauchi are drier northern states where desertification, not gully erosion, is the main hazard.
questions.p: Anambra State get soft sandy soil wey no dey strong, plus plenty rain wey dey fall for southeast, so gully erosion dey serious reach there. Sokoto, Borno and Bauchi dey north where desertification na di main wahala, no be gully erosion.

questions.q: Which of the following resources is classified as non-renewable because it takes millions of years to form and cannot be replenished within a human lifetime?
questions.e: Natural gas is a fossil fuel formed from decayed organic matter over millions of years, so once used up it cannot be quickly replaced. Wind, timber and fish can all regenerate or be renewed within a much shorter time.
questions.p: Natural gas na fossil fuel wey come from dead plant and animal wey don stay for ground plenty millions years, so once e finish e no fit quick come back. Wind, timber and fish fit renew within short time.

questions.q: Mangrove forests along the Niger Delta coastline help protect communities from coastal flooding and storm surges mainly because of which feature?
o: Their roots release oxygen that supports fish populations
Their tall trunks block strong winds from reaching the shore
Their leaves absorb carbon dioxide, reducing global warming
Their dense, tangled root systems reduce wave energy and trap sediments
questions.e: Mangrove roots form a thick tangled network along the shoreline that physically slows down incoming waves and traps sediments, reducing the force of storm surges on the land. Their trunks are not particularly tall, and carbon absorption or oxygen release does not directly stop flooding.
questions.p: Mangrove roots dey tangle well-well for shoreline, e dey slow down wave and trap sand, so di storm surge no go strong reach land. Di trunk no tall pass like dat, and carbon absorption or oxygen no be wetin dey directly stop flood.

questions.q: In population geography, population density is best defined as:
o: number of people per unit area of land
total number of people in a country
questions.e: Population density measures how many people live in a given unit area, usually expressed as persons per square kilometre. It is not the same as total population, growth rate, or migration figures.
questions.p: Population density na how many people dey live for one particular size of land, like per square kilometre. E no be di same thing as total population, growth rate, or migration number.

questions.q: The movement of people from rural villages to towns and cities mainly in search of jobs, education and better amenities is called:
questions.e: Rural-urban migration is movement within the same country from villages to cities. Transhumance and nomadism involve herders moving with animals, while emigration means leaving one's own country for another.
questions.p: Rural-urban migration na when people dey waka comot from village go city for better work, school and amenities. Transhumance and nomadism na about herdsmen and animals, while emigration na when person leave im country go another country.

questions.q: A town in Delta State has a population of 450,000 people and occupies a land area of 150 square kilometres. What is the population density of the town?
questions.e: Population density = population divided by land area = 450,000 / 150 = 3,000 persons per square kilometre.
questions.p: Population density na population divide by land area: 450,000 divide by 150 be 3,000 persons per square kilometre.

questions.q: Which of the following physical factors is most likely to encourage DENSE population settlement in an area?
questions.e: Fertile soil supports good crop yields and food security, attracting many settlers and farmers. Tsetse fly, volcanic eruptions and desert climate instead discourage settlement because they threaten health, safety, and farming.
questions.p: Fertile soil dey support good harvest and food, so e dey attract plenty people come settle. Tsetse fly, volcano and desert no good for health, safety and farming, so dem dey chase settlers comot.

questions.q: Which of the following is a PUSH factor responsible for migration of people from rural areas to urban centres?
o: High rate of unemployment in rural areas
Attraction of social amenities in towns
Presence of better educational facilities in the city
Availability of modern hospitals in urban centres
questions.e: Push factors are negative conditions in the place people are leaving, such as unemployment in rural areas. The other options describe attractive conditions in the city, which are pull factors, not push factors.
questions.p: Push factor na bad condition for di place wey person dey comot from, like unemployment for village. Di other options na good tins for city wey dey pull people go there, dem be pull factors not push factors.

questions.q: A country's population is growing at an annual rate of 3.5%. Using the rule of 70 (doubling time = 70 divided by growth rate), estimate how many years it will take for the population to double.
questions.e: Using the rule of 70: doubling time = 70 / 3.5 = 20 years. This simple method estimates how long a population needs to double at a constant growth rate.
questions.p: Use rule of 70: doubling time = 70 divide by 3.5 = 20 years. Dis method dey help estimate how long population go take double if growth rate no change.

questions.q: In a certain year, a country recorded a crude birth rate of 42 per 1000 people and a crude death rate of 14 per 1000 people. What was the rate of natural increase of the population, expressed as a percentage?
questions.e: Natural increase rate = (birth rate - death rate) / 1000 x 100 = (42 - 14) / 1000 x 100 = 2.8%. This shows the yearly growth from births and deaths only, ignoring migration.
questions.p: Natural increase rate = (birth rate minus death rate) divide by 1000 times 100 = (42 - 14)/1000 x 100 = 2.8%. Na di growth wey come from birth and death only, e no include migration.

questions.q: Fulani herdsmen in parts of Nigeria often move their cattle seasonally from the dry northern savanna to wetter southern grasslands in search of pasture and water, before returning home later in the year. This type of movement is called:
questions.e: Transhumance is the seasonal movement of pastoralists and their livestock between fixed areas to find pasture and water. Shifting cultivation involves farming, urbanization is growth of towns, and emigration is leaving one's country.
questions.p: Transhumance na when herdsmen and dia cattle dey waka seasonally between fixed places to find grass and water. Shifting cultivation na about farming, urbanization na growth of towns, and emigration na when person comot from im own country.

questions.q: Which of the following best defines a settlement in Geography?
o: A place where human beings live together permanently or semi-permanently while carrying out their daily activities
An area reserved exclusively for farming activities
A place where people reside temporarily only for trading purposes
A large city with more than one million inhabitants
